Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Miriam Chen (Redwood SE), Asha Patel (Halcyon Head of ML Infra), Tom Riley (Platform Eng), Leah Gomez (Security)
summary: Discovery focused on reliability patterns: multi-region routing, circuit-breaker behavior during degraded model performance, fallback to smaller models and cross-region fallthrough. Halcyon is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for an internal genomics annotation service; primary concerns are P99 latency, data residency, and auditability.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
SLA mapping (p99 vs availability), runbook integration
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for jumping on. Quick intros then we'll go into where you're seeing reliability pain today.
[00:08] Asha: Hi, Asha here - we run the in-house annotation pipeline, mostly finetuned open models, and latency spikes have been killing our user workflows.
[00:18] Tom: Yeah we've got heavy tail workloads, sometimes very long sequences from lab notes, and when the serving cluster gets saturated we see cascading timeouts.
[00:28] Miriam: Got it. Are those timeouts coming from the model side or network / infra?
[00:32] Asha: It's a mix. Roughly 60% resource pressure (GPU queueing), 30% network hiccups between regions, and 10% retries from the app layer.
[00:40] Jordan: Okay, so primary ask is resilience — graceful degradation when capacity is constrained. Curious — have you tried circuirt breakers or any rate limiting at the app side?
[00:50] Tom: We have a basic circuit-breaker in the app, but it's all-or-nothing. If model times out, we show fallback UI. We want something more surgical: fallback for specific heavy requests, or route to a cheaper model that returns best-effort.
[01:05] Miriam: That's exactly where Redwood's routing and model variants can help — you can set policy that routes by latency budget, and automatically fallback to a quantized/3B variant on overload.
[01:15] Leah: How deterministic is that? For regulated workloads we need audit logs, and we need to know when requests were handled by fallback models for quality auditing.
[01:24] Jordan: We store per-request routing metadata and a trace id; those appear in the console and in audit logs. We'll share a sample log format.
[01:30] Asha: Good. Also, data residency — some of our sequences are PHI-adjacent, we'll need private deployment or VPC options. Hosted is attractive but we need to understand the isolation guarantees.
[01:41] Jordan: Understood. Hosted can be ok for low-risk models but for PHI you probably want Private or Dedicated with VPC peering and customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). We have Private options that keep inference within your VPC and map to your KMS.
[01:53] Tom: If we go Private on prem or VPC, what changes in failure behavior? Do we still get automatic multi-region fallback?
[01:59] Miriam: If it's Private in a single region, automatic cross-region fallback is only possible if you enable a managed route to a Redwood region — that introduces egress constraints and policy decisions. For Dedicated (Redwood-run reserved pools) we can do cross-region failover with the same API surface.
[02:14] Asha: So in practice Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and built-in multi-region routing; Private gives you control but we have to wire the cross-region plan explicitly.
[02:24] Jordan: Right. Also worth considering model variants in the same region: degrade latency by switching to a smaller quantized model so you avoid cross-region hops. That often keeps latency within SLOs.
[02:34] Leah: For compliance we need: SOC 2, ISO certs, SSO via SAML + SCIM, RBAC, and full request-level audit. Do you have all that?
[02:44] Jordan: We do SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001; SSO/SAML and SCIM are supported, RBAC via console and API, and audit logs as mentioned. We'll attach the formal security pack.
[02:53] Tom: Cool. Metrics-wise, can Redwood do p99 latency SLOs? We aim for p99 < 350ms for interactive annotation.
[03:01] Miriam: Depends on model. For a 13B dense model p99 350ms at moderate load is tough; we typically recommend either a quantized 7B or batching/fast kernels. We can simulate with your traffic profile.
[03:14] Asha: We'd love a baseline: 10k requests per hour during peak, with average seq len 1.2k tokens and 95th at 3k. Can you ballpark cost and likely p99?
[03:25] Miriam: We'll run an estimate. Rough rules: at those seq lengths you pay more on token compute; switching to compiled kernels and using prefix caching for repeated prompts helps a ton. We should test with a pilot run.
[03:39] Jordan: On fallback policies — we often see customers want a tiered fallback: 1) retry on same model, 2) fallback to quantized variant, 3) route to secondary region, 4) degrade response (summary-only). You can set those priorities and time budgets per route.
[03:55] Tom: How are time budgets enforced? Is it client-side or server-side?
[03:58] Miriam: You set a budget in the routing policy; the router enforces server-side timeouts and can return a soft-degraded response or a special error to the app. Client-side can also do hedging.
[04:08] Leah: If we route to another region, how do you handle data egress and residency — we might need to mask or obfuscate PHI fields before crossing borders.
[04:18] Jordan: That's a common pattern — redaction pre-processing in your app before forwarding. Also we can restrict which request types are allowed cross-region.
[04:25] Asha: For audit, we'd like a flag on each request showing which fallbacks were used and why — helpful for downstream QA.
[04:32] Miriam: That exists in the routing trace; we'll export sample traces.
[04:36] Tom: On SLA — you're offering different SLAs for hosted vs dedicated?
[04:40] Jordan: Hosted has a standard uptime SLA but not the enterprise-level 99.99% dedicated SLA. Dedicated comes with committed capacity and better latency SLOs in the contract. Private is negotiated as part of enterprise licensing.
[04:51] Asha: Pricing sensitivity — if we have to provision dedicated GPUs for peak only, cost is a blocker. We need autoscaling plus burst policies.
[04:58] Miriam: Dedicated supports autoscaling with burst to shared capacity; you can set thresholds and costs are modeled into the pricing sheet we'll share. For pilot we usually recommend a small dedicated pool plus hosted fallback for bursts.
[05:10] Jordan: Quick note on KV cache — for repetitive prefixes across requests (like the same genomic header), prefix caching reduces compute per request massively. But cache invalidation is something we should plan for your finetuned models.
[05:23] Asha: Right, we have frequent model updates and need a rollout plan so cache is flushed or warmed appropriately.
[05:29] Miriam: Rollouts support canary and A/B; cache warming hooks are supported. We'll include a recommended rollout playbook.
[05:36] Tom: Any guidance on measurable SLOs vs SLA? We want to map internal SLOs (p95, p99 latency) to vendor SLA breach triggers.
[05:44] Jordan: We'll propose an SLO-to-SLA mapping: SLOs we monitor internally, and SLA is contractual availability; we can tie credits to sustained SLA violations at the contract level. We'll draft examples in the pilot sheet.
[05:54] Asha: Great. Next steps?
[05:57] Jordan: I'll send the pricing + pilot SLO worksheet; Miriam will run a p99 perf estimate; Asha will share traffic histograms. We'll reconvene after those artifacts to scope the pilot.
[06:06] Leah: Also please attach the security pack and sample audit log format.
[06:09] Jordan: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[06:12] (call ends)
